newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Key commodities turn volatile after rallies.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Key commodities turn volatile after rallies.

text.p: In a surprise show of strength on Friday, copper leapt to a nine-month high, leading prices for other base metals up, only to tumble lower late in the day.
Volatility reigned all week across commodities markets, and left a bull market in coffee - up 50 percent this year - faltering after a dazzling performance on Wednesday .
London copper traders said early sentiment was good with support from low stock levels and a strong New York opening which buoyed prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME).
But a late oscillation in copper futures saw the three-month contract fall to $2,389 at the close after peaking at $2,435.
Traders said copper suffered from end-week sales after speculative buying interest, which sparked the peak, faded.

"It's been a funny old day, and there has been no news whatsoever," said a London dealer. "The best thing you can say about copper is when it looks good you sell it, and when it looks bad you buy it."
Aluminium was pulled down by the red metal to close at $1,674, down $14 on the day.
The swings underpinned the recent indecisive air which saw both metals surge at the end of a lacklustre day on Thursday.
"I am convinced trends are upwards," said one floor-trader. "Dips are being bought at the moment."

Warehouse stocks fell by 6,225 tonnes as copper moved out of Italy, Singapore and the United States. Fundamentals also suggested copper demand would strengthen - Friday's U.S. payroll data indicated a strong economy with inflation in check.
Aluminium was initially hit by a smaller-than-expected stock fall of 1,800 tonnes, and recovered briefly before overhead selling pushed it lower.
But prices were not moved by a decision by Trans-World Group to stall investment in Russian aluminium pending a government decision on controlling foreign ownership of the industry.
World coffee prices also looked bearish, extending their downwards correction from peaks earlier in the week.
London's robusta futures ended $1 down on the day, despite clawing slightly higher at the close.
"There's no physical interest today for robustas," said one trader. "That's why they performed better towards the end of the day. The lower (price) levels attacted the industry buying."
Robusta futures for May closed at $1,729 per tonne, representing an eight percent slip from Wednesday's nine-month high. They earlier hit a low of $1,670.
Traders said robusta could come under further pressure from liquidation of long-positions in New York in the wake of Wednesday's 2-1/2 year high in U.S. benchmark arabica coffee.
Earlier, Uganda said it was cutting robusta coffee exports by over 200,000 60-kilo bags as part of an agreement by African producers to limit exports.
Asked whether export cuts were necessary in light of the explosion of robusta prices this year, a Ugandan coffee official said robusta prices still lagged behind arabica.
Analysts have said that coffee prices could be overdue for a pause. High prices have already prompted a number of roasters including France's Dowe Egberts to increase retail prices.
Precious metals also ended mixed in London after a nervous day's trading.
Gold closed at $348.80 compared to $351.95 on Thursday. Dealers said it was under pressure from weak technicals as well as Switzerland's plan to sell bullion to set up a fund for Holocaust victims.
Price swings in crude oil saw futures edge lower, trading at $20.00 a barrel at 1815 GMT, after forging ahead at the open.
Dealers in benchmark Brent oil said the market was split between those who believed the worst of the bearish trend was over and those who saw an overhang of physical crude.
Wheat and corn futures were firm on Friday and soybeans set contract highs on the Chicago Board of Trade after low stocks were predicted for 1997-98 by a private analytical firm.
This overshadowed news that a strike by Brazilian dockworkers which had helped propel soybean prices to a five-month high in Chicago, was halted on Friday - nearly 24-hours ahead of schedule.
The strike, in the key Brazilian grain port of Paranagua, began on Wednesday, and ended when a pay dispute was resolved with port operators.
